As dry summer weather continues to dry up public water supplies, city leaders have put strict limits on outdoor hose use, leaving many suburban lawns turning brown and dry. To keep their properties looking green all year round, a growing number of homeowners are choosing to rip out natural grass and install artificial turf instead.

Vancouver homeowner Sarah Jenkins recently put down fake grass in her front yard and couldn't be happier with her choice. "It is wonderful," Sarah explains. "I never have to worry about dragging heavy hoses around, I don't buy expensive bug sprays, and the yard always looks neat and bright green. It saves me so much time on my weekends."

However, city planners and engineers worry that a sudden rush toward plastic lawns could create unexpected problems for local neighborhoods. City official Dave Miller suggests that homeowners should be required to get a special local permit before putting down artificial grass, or risk paying a large fine. "Plastic turf has some nice benefits, but the materials do not absorb rainwater the way natural dirt does," Miller points out. "During sudden heavy rainstorms, water runs straight off these artificial surfaces too quickly, which can overload neighborhood drainage systems and cause street flooding."

Other residents argue that getting rid of natural soil and grass harms local ecosystems. Local gardener Liam Vance believes that fake lawns damage neighborhood wildlife. "Real grass and dirt provide necessary homes and food for earthworms, helpful insects, and local birds," Vance notes. "Furthermore, plastic mats trap summer heat and add more waste to local landfills when they wear out after several years."

Instead of plastic turf, Vance encourages people to plant hardy, low-water ground covers like creeping thyme, clover, or native mosses. "These plants handle dry summer conditions easily, need almost zero watering, and keep neighborhood bees and butterflies healthy," he adds.

As more communities look for smart ways to handle water shortages, homeowners are left trying to balance the clean convenience of fake grass against the long-term health of their local environment.
